title: Bolt a camera arm to a built T-slot frame: two hanging drop-in T-nuts go into the slot unseen, then swing under its lips
instruction: Mount the camera bracket on the frame bar that has the blue line, with its arm pointing in over the frame. Pick the bracket up by its arm and lower its foot onto the bar so that both drop-in T-nuts, hanging lengthwise under the foot, go down into the bar's slot, with the notch in the foot on the line. Keep hold of the arm and keep the foot flat on the bar: the camera end overhangs, and until a nut grips the bracket tips and its nuts lift out. With the other gripper take the T-handle hex driver from its block and tighten both screws until they are snug. As a screw starts to turn, its nut swings a quarter turn under the lips of the slot and is then drawn up tight. If a screw keeps turning without tightening, or goes tight while the foot is still loose, back it off and try again. Put the driver down, then let go of the bracket.
context: Frames of robot work cells and data-collection stations are built from T-slot profile, and cameras are bolted on afterwards: ALOHA 2's extrusion frame carries overhead and worm's-eye RealSense D405 cameras, and Trossen's assembly guide bolts the worm's-eye camera mount to the frame's front bar. On a built frame the slot ends are closed, so only drop-in nuts can be added (80/20: 'loads from profile end or side', 'ideal for captivated profiles'). Each nut has to pass the 8 mm opening lengthwise, out of sight under the bracket's foot: the foot's edges show the bar to a millimetre, the nuts need a fifth of that. It then turns a quarter turn under the lips as its screw is tightened (80/20's install drawings; item: the nut 'rotates around 90° and is clamped in the groove'), and if it does not catch, 'simply loosen the screw and try again' (FarmBot build guide, same kind of nut). Until a nut grips, the other hand must keep the overhanging arm level. Screws end snug, not torqued.
setup: Centimetres from the midpoint between the arm bases on the table top; x forward, y to the robot's left. Frame: four bars of 80/20 40-4040 T-slot profile (40 x 40 mm, clear anodised; each face has a slot 8.13 mm wide at the opening, with lips 4.32 mm thick over a cavity 20.57 mm wide and 12.32 mm deep), joined flat into a closed rectangle 36 (x) by 30 (y) with an 80/20 40-4302 inside corner bracket in each corner, fastened to the table through the bars' bottom slots, top 4 cm up. Cross bars along y at x 10 and x 42; side bars between them along x at y -8 (right) and y 18, so both ends of each side bar's top slot are closed. A blue paint-pen line 6 mm wide crosses the right bar's top and outer face at x 24. Camera bracket, 168 g with camera and hardware, printed solid in grey PETG (drawing and model in the task folder): a foot 80 x 40 x 6.4 mm with a V notch in the middle of one long edge and two 6.0 mm holes 60 mm apart, a light push fit on the screws; an arm 20 x 12 mm from the other long edge to 200 mm from the foot's centre, undersides flush; a side plate at the arm's end carrying an Intel RealSense D405 (42 x 42 x 23 mm, 60 g, fixed by its two M3 back threads, lens level; a block of that size and mass will do), its top level with the arm's and hanging 30 mm below it: the low, worm's-eye camera of a work cell. In each hole an M6 x 16 socket head cap screw with an 80/20 3931 drop-in T-nut (15.75 x 7.75 x 6.07 mm; with the screw, 80/20 bolt assembly 75-3595), one turn of thread-seal tape on the thread, the nut threaded on until the screw's end is flush with its underside, long side along the foot's long side. The bracket waits left of the frame on three EVA foam blocks 35 mm high, so that nuts and camera hang free: foot centred at (33, 29), arm pointing toward the robot. Driver: Wera 454 HF T-handle hex key 5 x 100 mm (79 g) standing blade down in a 7 mm hole 35 mm deep in a beech block 60 x 60 x 40 mm fixed at (20, -25), handle along x, short arm toward the robot. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Read at the end of the run. Any score above 0 needs both grippers and the driver at least 1 cm clear of the bracket and the bracket still for 1 s. A nut grips when it lies crosswise under both lips of the marked bar's slot (each end at least 1 mm under its lip), drawn up against them, and its screw has turned at least a quarter turn past the point where the nut met the lips. 1.0: both nuts grip, the arm points in over the frame, and the notch's point is within 2 mm of the middle of the line. 0.75: the same with the notch 2 to 5 mm from it. 0.5: exactly one nut grips, or both grip with the notch more than 5 mm off or the arm pointing outward. 0.25: no nut grips, but both nuts are in the marked bar's slot (tops at least 1 mm below the bar's face), whether the foot lies flat or the bracket has tipped onto its camera end. 0: anything else. Which screw is driven first, which hand does what and where the driver is put down are free. Real trial: ruler from the middle of the line to the notch. Then test each nut by the bracket's own overhang: take the other screw right out. A nut that grips keeps the foot flat on the bar (a 0.5 mm feeler goes under no corner); one that does not lets the camera end drop. Put that screw back snug and test the other nut the same way.
reset_notes: Take both screws out and lift the bracket off. Put each screw back through its hole and thread its nut on until the screw's end is flush with the nut's underside (renew the turn of thread-seal tape when the nut starts to swing freely). Set the nuts lengthwise: stand the foot on a 5 cm offcut of the same profile with both nuts in its slot and turn each screw anticlockwise until its nut stops. Lift the bracket by its arm onto the three foam blocks, arm toward the robot, and stand the driver in its block. Check that the frame has not moved. About 2 minutes. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at real size. Slot lips, walls and floor and each nut's flange and boss collide; nothing guides or places a nut. Each screw is a hinge in the foot (20 mN m drag), turned only by the driver's hex in its socket. Each nut rides its screw on a rule: thread friction (10 mN m) carries it round until contact stops it, then 1 mm of travel per turn on a 40 N/mm thread, torque rising with clamp load. No thread play: nut colliders are 0.3 mm narrower. Lip ridges and camera cable not modelled.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (3,600 steps, no refusal: it took the driver out of its block and laid it on the table; the bracket never left its foam blocks); demo: 1.0 (scripted, success at step 2,217 of 3,600)
